notes.front: What are unprotected sides and edges, in Subpart M?
notes.back: Any side or edge of a walking/working surface, such as a floor or roof, with no wall or guardrail system at least 39 inches high.
notes.explanation: Entrances to points of access are excluded from the definition.
notes.example: Like the open side of a new mezzanine floor before any rail or wall goes up.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 290
notes.evidence: Unprotected sides and edges means any side or edge (except at entrances to points of access) of a walking/working surface, e.g., floor, roof, ramp, or runway where there is no wall or guardrail system at least 39 inches (1.0 m) high.

notes.front: What is a leading edge, in Subpart M?
notes.back: The edge of a floor, roof or formwork that changes location as more floor, roof, decking or formwork sections are placed.
notes.explanation: When it is not actively and continuously under construction, a leading edge counts as an unprotected side and edge.
notes.example: Like the front of a metal deck that creeps forward sheet by sheet as the crew lays it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 289
notes.evidence: Leading edge means the edge of a floor, roof, or formwork for a floor or other walking/working surface (such as the deck) which changes location as additional floor, roof, decking, or formwork sections are placed, formed, or constructed.

notes.front: What is a hole, in Subpart M?
notes.back: A gap or void 2 inches or more in its least dimension, in a floor, roof or other walking/working surface.
notes.explanation: The smallest dimension decides: a long narrow slot under 2 inches wide is not a hole under this definition.
notes.example: Like an opening left in a slab for a future duct or stair.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 289
notes.evidence: Hole means a gap or void 2 inches (5.1 cm) or more in its least dimension, in a floor, roof, or other walking/working surface.

notes.front: What is a guardrail system?
notes.back: A barrier erected to prevent employees from falling to lower levels.
notes.explanation: Subpart M's definition names no parts, because § 1926.502(b) separately sets the heights and strengths of top rails and midrails.
notes.example: Like the railing round a balcony, but built to set heights and strengths for a work area.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 289
notes.evidence: Guardrail system means a barrier erected to prevent employees from falling to lower levels.

notes.front: What is a safety net system used for in fall protection?
notes.back: A net installed under the work surface to catch a falling employee, as close as practicable and never more than 30 feet below.
notes.explanation: Subpart M names safety nets alongside guardrails and personal fall arrest systems as a conventional fall protection system.
notes.example: Like a circus net under a trapeze, strung beneath a bridge deck under construction.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(c)(1), p. 294
notes.evidence: Safety nets shall be installed as close as practicable under the walking/ working surface on which employees are working, but in no case more than 30 feet (9.1 m) below such level.

notes.front: What is a personal fall arrest system (PFAS)?
notes.back: A system to arrest an employee in a fall: an anchorage, connectors and a body harness, perhaps with a lanyard, deceleration device or lifeline.
notes.explanation: Subpart M’s definition also allows a body belt, but prohibits its use for fall arrest from 1 January 1998.
notes.example: Like a climber’s harness and rope tied to a bolt, which stops the climber after a slip.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 290
notes.evidence: Personal fall arrest system means a system used to arrest an employee in a fall from a working level. It consists of an anchorage, connectors, a body belt or body harness and may include a lanyard, deceleration device, lifeline, or suitable combinations of these.

notes.front: What is a positioning device system?
notes.back: A body belt or harness rigged to support an employee on an elevated vertical surface, such as a wall, working hands-free while leaning.
notes.explanation: It holds the worker in place for the task rather than arresting a fall.
notes.example: Like a lineman leaning back in a strap round a pole to work with both hands.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 290
notes.evidence: Positioning device system means a body belt or body harness system rigged to allow an employee to be supported on an elevated vertical surface, such as a wall, and work with both hands free while leaning.

notes.front: What is a warning line system?
notes.back: A barrier on a roof warning employees they are nearing an unprotected edge, marking an area where roofing can proceed without guardrails, belts or nets.
notes.explanation: Subpart M lets it be used on low-slope roofs only in combination with another system.
notes.example: Like a rope-and-flag line on a flat roof keeping the roofers’ work area back from the edge.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 290
notes.evidence: Warning line system means a barrier erected on a roof to warn employees that they are approaching an unprotected roof side or edge, and which designates an area in which roofing work may take place without the use of guardrail, body belt, or safety net systems

notes.front: What is a safety monitoring system?
notes.back: A safety system in which a competent person is responsible for recognising and warning employees of fall hazards.
notes.explanation: It relies on a person watching, not on a physical barrier or harness.
notes.example: Like a lifeguard for a roofing crew: watching, and shouting a warning before someone steps too near the edge.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 290
notes.evidence: Safety-monitoring system means a safety system in which a competent person is responsible for recognizing and warning employees of fall hazards.

notes.front: What is a controlled access zone (CAZ)?
notes.back: An area where certain work, such as overhand bricklaying, may take place without guardrails, fall arrest or nets, with access to the zone controlled.
notes.explanation: Subpart M allows it for overhand bricklaying and in fall protection plans for leading edge work.
notes.example: Like a roped-off strip of floor that only the bricklaying crew may enter.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 288
notes.evidence: Controlled access zone (CAZ) means an area in which certain work (e.g., overhand bricklaying) may take place without the use of guardrail systems, personal fall arrest systems, or safety net systems and access to the zone is controlled.

notes.front: What is falling object protection, under section 1926.501(c)?
notes.back: A hard hat for each exposed employee, plus toeboards, screens or guardrails; a canopy; or a barricaded area below.
notes.explanation: The employer picks one of the three measures, and the hard hat is required in every case.
notes.example: Like a covered walkway past a building site, plus hard hats for anyone under the work.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(c), p. 293
notes.evidence: When an employee is exposed to falling objects, the employer shall have each employee wear a hard hat and shall implement one of the following measures

notes.front: Each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge {{c1::6 feet}} or more above a lower level must be protected from falling.
notes.explanation: The protection must be a guardrail system, safety net system or personal fall arrest system.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(1), p. 291
notes.evidence: with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems

notes.front: What must the employer determine about a walking/working surface before employees work on it?
notes.back: That it has the strength and structural integrity to support them safely.
notes.explanation: Employees may work on it only when it has that strength and integrity.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(a)(2), p. 291
notes.evidence: The employer shall determine if the walking/working surfaces on which its employees are to work have the strength and structural integrity to support employees safely.

notes.front: How must an employee constructing a leading edge 6 feet or more above lower levels be protected?
notes.back: By guardrail systems, safety net systems or personal fall arrest systems, unless a fall protection plan is justified.
notes.explanation: The plan is allowed only where the employer shows these systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(2)(i), p. 291
notes.evidence: Each employee who is constructing a leading edge 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above lower levels shall be protected from falling by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.

notes.front: Who bears the burden of showing that conventional fall protection is infeasible, so a fall protection plan may be used?
notes.back: The employer; Subpart M presumes at least one conventional system is feasible and creates no greater hazard.
notes.explanation: The presumption sits in a note to the leading edge, precast and residential duties.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(2) note, p. 291
notes.evidence: There is a presumption that it is feasible and will not create a greater hazard to implement at least one of the above-listed fall protection systems. Accordingly, the employer has the burden of establishing

notes.front: In a hoist area, what protection does an employee need when a guardrail section is removed and he must lean out through the opening?
notes.back: A personal fall arrest system.
notes.explanation: Otherwise hoist areas need guardrail systems or personal fall arrest systems at 6 feet or more.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(3), p. 291
notes.evidence: that employee shall be protected from fall hazards by a personal fall arrest system

notes.front: How must employees be protected from falling through holes, including skylights, more than 6 feet above lower levels?
notes.back: By personal fall arrest systems, covers, or guardrail systems erected around the holes.
notes.explanation: Covers are also required to stop people tripping into holes and objects falling through them.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(4)(i), p. 291
notes.evidence: shall be protected from falling through holes (including skylights) more than 6 feet (1.8 m) above lower levels, by personal fall arrest systems, covers, or guardrail systems erected around such holes

notes.front: Which three systems may protect an employee on the face of formwork or reinforcing steel from a fall of 6 feet or more?
notes.back: Personal fall arrest systems, safety net systems, or positioning device systems.
notes.explanation: Positioning device systems are listed here as an alternative to fall arrest systems and nets.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(5), p. 291
notes.evidence: Each employee on the face of formwork or reinforcing steel shall be protected from falling 6 feet (1.8 m) or more to lower levels by personal fall arrest systems, safety net systems, or positioning device systems.

notes.front: What protection does Subpart M require for employees on ramps, runways and other walkways 6 feet or more above lower levels?
notes.back: Guardrail systems.
notes.explanation: Guardrails are the only option listed for these surfaces.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(6), p. 291
notes.evidence: Each employee on ramps, runways, and other walkways shall be protected from falling 6 feet (1.8 m) or more to lower levels by guardrail systems.

notes.front: How must an employee less than 6 feet above dangerous equipment be protected?
notes.back: By guardrail systems or equipment guards, against falling into or onto the equipment.
notes.explanation: Here the 6-foot trigger does not apply; at 6 feet or more, the usual three systems are required.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(8)(i), p. 292
notes.evidence: Each employee less than 6 feet (1.8 m) above dangerous equipment shall be protected from falling into or onto the dangerous equipment by guardrail systems or by equipment guards.

notes.front: Besides the three conventional systems, what option does Subpart M give for overhand bricklaying 6 feet or more above lower levels?
notes.back: Working in a controlled access zone.
notes.explanation: An employee reaching more than 10 inches below the working surface still needs a guardrail, net or personal fall arrest system.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(9)(i), p. 292
notes.evidence: shall be protected from falling by guardrail systems, safety net systems, personal fall arrest systems, or shall work in a controlled access zone

notes.front: What is a low-slope roof, in Subpart M?
notes.back: A roof with a slope less than or equal to 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal).
notes.explanation: A roof steeper than 4 in 12 is a steep roof, with its own protection rule.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 289
notes.evidence: Low-slope roof means a roof having a slope less than or equal to 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal).

notes.front: On a low-slope roof, which system may be combined with a warning line system to protect roofers at edges 6 feet or more up?
notes.back: Any one of: a guardrail system, safety net system, personal fall arrest system or safety monitoring system.
notes.explanation: The roofers may also use guardrails, nets or personal fall arrest alone, without a warning line.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(10), p. 292
notes.evidence: or a combination of warning line system and guardrail system, warning line system and safety net system, or warning line system and personal fall arrest system, or warning line system and safety monitoring system

notes.front: On low-slope roofs {{c1::50 feet}} or less in width, a safety monitoring system alone, without a warning line, is permitted.
notes.explanation: On wider roofs a safety monitoring system must be paired with a warning line system.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(10), p. 292
notes.evidence: on roofs 50-feet (15.25 m) or less in width (see appendix A to subpart M of this part), the use of a safety monitoring system alone [i.e. without the warning line system] is permitted

notes.front: How must an employee on a steep roof with unprotected edges 6 feet or more up be protected?
notes.back: By guardrail systems with toeboards, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.
notes.explanation: Warning lines and safety monitors are not options on a steep roof.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(11), p. 292
notes.evidence: Each employee on a steep roof with unprotected sides and edges 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above lower levels shall be protected from falling by guardrail systems with toeboards, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.

notes.front: At what height must employees in residential construction be protected by guardrails, nets or personal fall arrest?
notes.back: 6 feet or more above lower levels.
notes.explanation: A fall protection plan is allowed where the employer shows the systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(13), p. 292
notes.evidence: Each employee engaged in residential construction activities 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above lower levels shall be protected by guardrail systems, safety net system, or personal fall arrest system

notes.front: The top edge of a guardrail system’s top rail must be {{c1::42 inches plus or minus 3 inches}} above the walking/working level.
notes.explanation: When employees use stilts, the top-edge height must rise by the height of the stilts.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(b)(1), p. 293
notes.evidence: Top edge height of top rails, or equivalent guardrail system members, shall be 42 inches (1.1 m) plus or minus 3 inches (8 cm) above the walking/

notes.front: When must a guardrail system have midrails, screens, mesh or equivalent members, and where do midrails go?
notes.back: When there is no wall or parapet at least 21 inches high; midrails go midway between the top edge and the working level.
notes.explanation: Screens and mesh, when used, must extend from the top rail to the walking/working level.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(b)(2)(i), p. 293
notes.evidence: Midrails, when used, shall be installed at a height midway between the top edge of the guardrail system and the walking/working level.

notes.front: What force must a guardrail system withstand at its top edge?
notes.back: At least 200 pounds, applied within 2 inches of the top edge in any outward or downward direction.
notes.explanation: Under that downward load, the top edge must not deflect below 39 inches above the working level.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(b)(3), p. 293
notes.evidence: Guardrail systems shall be capable of withstanding, without failure, a force of at least 200 pounds (890 N) applied within 2 inches (5.1 cm) of the top edge, in any outward or downward direction

notes.front: What force must midrails, screens and other intermediate members withstand?
notes.back: At least 150 pounds applied in any downward or outward direction at any point along them.
notes.explanation: This is lower than the 200 pounds required at the top edge.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(b)(5), p. 293
notes.evidence: shall be capable of withstanding, without failure, a force of at least 150 pounds (666 N) applied in any downward

notes.front: What may not be used as top rails or midrails?
notes.back: Steel banding and plastic banding.
notes.explanation: Top rails and midrails must also be at least a quarter of an inch thick to prevent cuts and lacerations.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(b)(8), p. 294
notes.evidence: Steel banding and plastic banding shall not be used as top rails or midrails.

notes.front: What is the greatest distance a safety net may be installed below the working surface?
notes.back: 30 feet; it must be as close as practicable.
notes.explanation: The net must also extend outward from the edge by 8 to 13 feet, depending on the vertical drop.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(c)(1), p. 294
notes.evidence: but in no case more than 30 feet (9.1 m) below such level

notes.front: What is the drop test for a safety net installation?
notes.back: A 400-pound bag of sand, 30 ± 2 inches across, dropped into the net from at least 42 inches above the highest walking/working surface.
notes.explanation: The test is done after installation, when relocated, after major repair and every 6 months if left in place.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(c)(4)(i), p. 294
notes.evidence: dropped into the net from the highest walking/working surface at which employees are exposed to fall hazards, but not from less than 42 inches (1.1 m) above that level

notes.front: How often must safety nets be inspected for wear, damage and deterioration?
notes.back: At least once a week, and after any occurrence that could affect the net’s integrity.
notes.explanation: Defective nets must not be used, and defective components must be removed from service.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(c)(5), p. 295
notes.evidence: Safety nets shall be inspected at least once a week for wear, damage, and other deterioration.

notes.front: Since 1 January 1998, may a body belt be part of a personal fall arrest system?
notes.back: No. Body belts are not acceptable in a personal fall arrest system; a body harness is used.
notes.explanation: A body belt may still be used in a positioning device system.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d), p. 295
notes.evidence: Effective January 1, 1998, body belts are not acceptable as part of a personal fall arrest system.

notes.front: What load must an anchorage for personal fall arrest equipment support, if not designed by a qualified person?
notes.back: At least 5,000 pounds per employee attached, independent of any anchorage supporting platforms.
notes.explanation: The alternative is a complete system with a safety factor of at least two, used under a qualified person’s supervision.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(15), p. 296
notes.evidence: shall be independent of any anchorage being used to support or suspend platforms and capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds (22.2 kN) per employee attached

notes.front: How far may an employee free fall in a personal fall arrest system?
notes.back: No more than 6 feet, and without contacting any lower level.
notes.explanation: The system must be rigged to meet both limits.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(16)(iii), p. 296
notes.evidence: be rigged such that an employee can neither free fall more than 6 feet (1.8 m), nor contact any lower level

notes.front: What is the maximum deceleration distance allowed when a personal fall arrest system stops a fall?
notes.back: 3.5 feet.
notes.explanation: The system must bring the employee to a complete stop within that distance.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(16)(iv), p. 296
notes.evidence: bring an employee to a complete stop and limit maximum deceleration distance an employee travels to 3.5 feet (1.07 m)

notes.front: What is the maximum arresting force on an employee in a personal fall arrest system with a body harness?
notes.back: 1,800 pounds.
notes.explanation: The figure with a body belt was 900 pounds.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(16)(ii), p. 296
notes.evidence: limit maximum arresting force on an employee to 1,800 pounds (8 kN) when used with a body harness

notes.front: Since 1 January 1998, which type of snaphook may be used in a personal fall arrest system?
notes.back: Only the locking type.
notes.explanation: Unless designed for it, a snaphook must not be engaged to webbing, rope, another snaphook or a horizontal lifeline, among others.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(5), p. 295
notes.evidence: Effective January 1, 1998, only locking type snaphooks shall be used.

notes.front: What happens to a personal fall arrest system after it has arrested a fall?
notes.back: It is removed from service at once and not reused until a competent person inspects it and finds it undamaged.
notes.explanation: Components subjected to impact loading are covered by the same rule.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(19), p. 296
notes.evidence: Personal fall arrest systems and components subjected to impact loading shall be immediately removed from service and shall not be used again for employee protection until inspected and determine

notes.front: When must personal fall arrest systems be inspected for wear, damage and deterioration?
notes.back: Prior to each use; defective components are removed from service.
notes.explanation: This is separate from the inspection needed after a system arrests a fall.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(21), p. 296
notes.evidence: Personal fall arrest systems shall be inspected prior to each use for wear, damage and other deterioration, and defective components shall be removed from service.

notes.front: What must the employer provide for in case an employee falls in a personal fall arrest system?
notes.back: Prompt rescue, or assurance that employees can rescue themselves.
notes.explanation: The duty sits beside the rules on inspecting and removing a system after it has arrested a fall.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(20), p. 296
notes.evidence: The employer shall provide for prompt rescue of employees in the event of a fall or shall assure that employees are able to rescue themselves.

notes.front: May a personal fall arrest system be attached to a guardrail system?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Subpart M forbids attaching personal fall arrest systems to guardrail systems.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(23), p. 296
notes.evidence: Personal fall arrest systems shall not be attached to guardrail systems

notes.front: How far may a positioning device let an employee free fall?
notes.back: No more than 2 feet.
notes.explanation: Positioning devices must also be secured to an anchorage of stated strength.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(e)(1), p. 297
notes.evidence: Positioning devices shall be rigged such that an employee cannot free fall more than 2 feet (.6 m).

notes.front: When no mechanical equipment is used, how far from the roof edge must a warning line be erected?
notes.back: Not less than 6 feet.
notes.explanation: With mechanical equipment, it rises to 10 feet from edges perpendicular to the direction of operation.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(f)(1)(i), p. 297
notes.evidence: When mechanical equipment is not being used, the warning line shall be erected not less than 6 feet (1.8 m) from the roof edge.

notes.front: What are two requirements for where a safety monitor stands relative to the employee being monitored?
notes.back: On the same walking/working surface within visual sighting distance; and close enough to communicate orally.
notes.explanation: The monitor must also have no other duties that could distract from monitoring.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(h)(1), p. 299
notes.evidence: The safety monitor shall be on the same walking/working surface and within visual sighting distance of the employee being monitored; (iv) The safety monitor shall be close enough to communicate orally with the employee

notes.front: What two requirements apply to all hole covers, besides their strength?
notes.back: Secured against displacement by wind, equipment or employees; colour coded or marked “hole” or “cover”.
notes.explanation: Covers outside roadways must support at least twice the weight of employees, equipment and materials on them at one time.
notes.evidence: All covers shall be secured when installed so as to prevent accidental displacement by the wind, equipment, or employees. (4) All covers shall be color coded or they shall be marked with the word ‘‘HOLE’’ or ‘‘COVER’’

notes.front: What load must a cover in a roadway or vehicular aisle support without failure?
notes.back: At least twice the maximum axle load of the largest vehicle expected to cross it.
notes.explanation: Other covers are rated by twice the weight of employees, equipment and materials that may be on them.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(i)(1), p. 299
notes.evidence: Covers located in roadways and vehicular aisles shall be capable of supporting, without failure, at least twice the maximum axle load of the largest vehicle expected to cross over the cover.

notes.front: What is the minimum height of a toeboard used as falling object protection?
notes.back: 3½ inches, with no more than ¼ inch clearance above the walking/working surface.
notes.explanation: Toeboards must also withstand at least 50 pounds and be solid or have openings no larger than 1 inch.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(j)(3), p. 299
notes.evidence: Toeboards shall be a minimum of 31⁄2 inches (9 cm) in vertical height from their top edge to the level of the walking/working surface.

notes.front: For which three kinds of work is a fall protection plan an option, and who must prepare it?
notes.back: Leading edge work, precast concrete erection and residential construction; a qualified person prepares it.
notes.explanation: The plan must be site-specific and kept up to date; the employer must show conventional protection is infeasible or more hazardous.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(k), p. 300
notes.evidence: This option is available only to employees engaged in leading edge work, precast concrete erection work, or residential construction work

notes.front: Who must train employees who might be exposed to fall hazards, under section 1926.503?
notes.back: A competent person qualified in the listed areas, such as the nature of fall hazards in the work area.
notes.explanation: The programme must enable each employee to recognise fall hazards and follow procedures that minimise them.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.503(a)(2), p. 300
notes.evidence: The employer shall assure that each employee has been trained, as necessary, by a competent person qualified in the following areas: (i) The nature of fall hazards in the work area

notes.front: What must the written certification record of fall protection training contain?
notes.back: The trained employee’s name or identity; the date(s) of training; the signature of the trainer or the employer.
notes.explanation: The latest training certification must be kept.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.503(b)(1), p. 301
notes.evidence: The written certification record shall contain the name or other identity of the employee trained, the date(s) of the training, and the signature of the person who conducted the training or the signature of the employer.

notes.front: What are two circumstances in which fall protection retraining is required?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: workplace changes make training obsolete; new types of system or equipment; the employee shows inadequate knowledge or skill.
notes.explanation: The duty arises when the employer has reason to believe a trained employee lacks the understanding and skill required.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.503(c), p. 301
notes.evidence: Circumstances where retraining is required include, but are not limited to, situations where: (1) Changes in the workplace render previous training obsolete

notes.front: A carpenter frames walls on a second floor whose open edge is 9 feet above the ground. Which of these meets Subpart M?
notes.back: C: a guardrail system, safety net or personal fall arrest system.
notes.choices:
A) A warning line 6 feet back
B) A safety monitor
C) A guardrail system, safety net or personal fall arrest system
D) Nothing, because it is under 10 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are roofing options on low-slope roofs, not for floor edges. D: 10 feet is the scaffold trigger; Subpart M uses 6 feet.
notes.explanation: The edge is at least 6 feet above a lower level, so one of the three conventional systems is required.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(b)(1), p. 291
notes.evidence: Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling

notes.front: A 3-foot square opening in a slab is covered with a loose plywood sheet, unmarked, that people walk over. What is wrong?
notes.back: D: the cover must be secured and colour coded or marked “hole” or “cover”.
notes.choices:
A) Covers are only needed on roofs
B) Nothing; plywood is always acceptable
C) Only openings under 2 inches need covers
D) The cover must be secured and colour coded or marked “hole” or “cover”
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores securing and marking. C reverses the definition: a hole is 2 inches or more. A: covers apply to floors, roofs and other walking/working surfaces.
notes.explanation: The opening is a hole, and its cover must also support twice the load that may be on it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(i)(3), p. 299
notes.evidence: All covers shall be secured when installed so as to prevent accidental displacement by the wind, equipment, or employees.

notes.front: A new guardrail’s top edge measures 37 inches above the deck, and there is no midrail or wall. What is wrong?
notes.back: A: the top rail is too low, and a midrail or equivalent is needed.
notes.choices:
A) The top rail is too low and a midrail or equivalent is needed
B) Nothing
C) Only the missing midrail
D) Only the height, which must be exactly 42 inches
notes.choicesExplained: B: 37 inches is below the 39-inch minimum. C misses the height. D: the rule allows 42 inches plus or minus 3.
notes.explanation: Without a wall or parapet at least 21 inches high, midrails, screens or equivalent members are required.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(b)(2), p. 293
notes.evidence: Midrails, screens, mesh, intermediate vertical members, or equivalent intermediate structural members shall be installed between the top edge of the guardrail system and the walking/working surface when there is no wall or parapet wall at least 21 inches (53 cm) high.

notes.front: An ironworker arrives with a body belt and lanyard to use for fall arrest at a 20-foot edge. What should the foreman say?
notes.back: B: use a body harness; body belts are not acceptable for fall arrest.
notes.choices:
A) Fine, a belt is a personal fall arrest system
B) Use a body harness; body belts are not acceptable for fall arrest
C) Fine, if the lanyard is short
D) Use the belt with a second lanyard
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D all keep the body belt as fall arrest, which Subpart M has not accepted since 1998.
notes.explanation: A body belt may still serve in a positioning device system, which is not fall arrest.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 290
notes.evidence: As of January 1, 1998, the use of a body belt for fall arrest is prohibited.

notes.front: Two workers want to tie off to one anchorage that no qualified person has designed. What must it support?
notes.back: A: 10,000 pounds, that is 5,000 per employee attached.
notes.choices:
A) 10,000 pounds, that is 5,000 per employee attached
B) 3,600 pounds
C) 1,800 pounds per worker
D) 5,000 pounds in total
notes.choicesExplained: D counts only one worker. B is the snaphook proof-test load. C is the arresting-force limit with a harness.
notes.explanation: The 5,000-pound figure applies per employee attached.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(15), p. 296
notes.evidence: capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds (22.2 kN) per employee attached

notes.front: A system allows 6 feet of free fall and 3.5 feet of deceleration. The worker stands on a platform 8 feet above the ground. What is the problem?
notes.back: D: the worker could hit the ground, which the system must prevent.
notes.choices:
A) There is no problem
B) The free fall exceeds the limit
C) The deceleration exceeds the limit
D) The worker could hit the ground, which the system must prevent
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are each at, not over, their limits. A ignores that 9.5 feet of fall and stopping distance exceeds the 8 feet available.
notes.explanation: The system must be rigged so the employee cannot contact any lower level.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(16)(iii), p. 296
notes.evidence: be rigged such that an employee can neither free fall more than 6 feet (1.8 m), nor contact any lower level

notes.front: A roofer falls and hangs in his harness; the lanyard’s shock absorber has deployed. What does Subpart M require?
notes.back: D: rescue him promptly, and take the system out of service until a competent person inspects it.
notes.choices:
A) Inspect the system at the end of the week
B) Let him wait for the fire service, then reuse the lanyard
C) Reuse the system if it looks fine to him
D) Rescue him promptly, and take the system out of service until a competent person inspects it
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores prompt rescue and reuse limits. C: only a competent person may clear it. A: removal must be immediate.
notes.explanation: Both the rescue duty and the impact-loading rule apply after any arrested fall.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(d)(19), p. 296
notes.evidence: shall be immediately removed from service and shall not be used again for employee protection until inspected and determine

notes.front: Labourers work at ground level beneath a scaffold where bricks are stacked. Which set of measures meets section 1926.501(c)?
notes.back: C: hard hats, plus toeboards, screens or guardrails to stop objects falling.
notes.choices:
A) A warning sign only
B) Hard hats alone
C) Hard hats, plus toeboards, screens or guardrails to stop objects falling
D) Toeboards alone, without hard hats
notes.choicesExplained: A is not a listed measure. B and D each leave out half of the requirement: hard hats and one of the listed measures.
notes.explanation: A canopy or a barricaded area below are the other two listed measures.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.501(c)(1), p. 293
notes.evidence: Erect toeboards, screens, or guardrail systems to prevent objects from falling from higher levels

notes.front: A roof rises 6 inches for every 12 inches horizontally. Which protection options apply to roofers at its 20-foot edges?
notes.back: A: guardrails with toeboards, safety nets or personal fall arrest.
notes.choices:
A) Guardrails with toeboards, safety nets or personal fall arrest
B) Safety monitor alone
C) Warning line with a safety monitor
D) Warning line alone
notes.choicesExplained: C and B are options only on low-slope roofs, of 4 in 12 or less. D is never enough alone.
notes.explanation: A slope of 6 in 12 is greater than 4 in 12, so it is a steep roof.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.500(b), p. 290
notes.evidence: Steep roof means a roof having a slope greater than 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal).

notes.front: A new crew will use nets and harnesses on a bridge deck. Who may train them in fall hazards and in using the systems?
notes.back: D: a competent person qualified in those areas.
notes.choices:
A) Anyone who has read the manual
B) The crane operator
C) The newest employee on site
D) A competent person qualified in those areas
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are not tied to the competence Subpart M requires of the trainer.
notes.explanation: The employer then verifies the training with a written certification record.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.503(a)(2), p. 300
notes.evidence: The employer shall assure that each employee has been trained, as necessary, by a competent person qualified in the following areas

notes.front: A precast erector says harnesses and nets are impossible for one lift and wants to work under a fall protection plan. What must happen first?
notes.back: D: the employer shows the systems are infeasible or more hazardous, and a qualified person prepares a site-specific plan.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; plans are allowed for any work
B) The foreman signs a waiver
C) The crew uses a warning line
D) The employer shows the systems are infeasible or more hazardous, and a qualified person prepares a site-specific plan
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are not recognised alternatives. A: plans are limited to leading edge, precast and residential work.
notes.explanation: Subpart M presumes conventional systems are feasible, so the burden lies on the employer.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(k)(1), p. 300
notes.evidence: The fall protection plan shall be prepared by a qualified person and developed specifically for the site where the leading edge work, precast concrete work, or residential construction work is being performed

notes.front: How does a positioning device system differ from a personal fall arrest system in the free fall it allows?
notes.back: Positioning devices allow no more than 2 feet of free fall; a personal fall arrest system allows up to 6 feet.
notes.explanation: A positioning device holds the worker at the work; a fall arrest system stops a fall already under way.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(e)(1), p. 297
notes.evidence: Positioning devices shall be rigged such that an employee cannot free fall more than 2 feet (.6 m).

notes.front: How does a warning line system differ from a safety monitoring system?
notes.back: A warning line is a physical barrier set back from the roof edge; safety monitoring relies on a competent person watching and warning.
notes.explanation: On low-slope roofs the two may be combined, and on roofs 50 feet wide or less a monitor may work alone.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.502(h)(1), p. 299
notes.evidence: The employer shall designate a competent person to monitor the safety of other employees
